passage: Cities are often described as collections of buildings, roads, and services. Yet their resilience depends just as much on less visible systems: social trust, access to information, and the ability of institutions to learn. When a flood occurs, for example, a technically accurate warning may still fail if residents do not understand it or do not trust the source. Conversely, local networks can help information reach vulnerable households quickly. This does not mean that community action can replace public infrastructure. Rather, resilience emerges when reliable infrastructure, clear communication, and local knowledge reinforce one another. Planning for uncertainty therefore requires more than predicting a single future. It requires building systems that can adapt when assumptions prove wrong.

content: What is the main purpose of Reading Text B?
options: To argue that measurable indicators should never be used.
To explain the usefulness and limitations of proxies in evaluating complex phenomena.
To compare school attendance with hospital costs.
To show that all institutions manipulate their data.
passage: In many fields, researchers rely on proxies: observable measures used to represent concepts that are difficult to measure directly. A school may use attendance as an indicator of engagement; a public-health agency may use hospital admissions to estimate disease burden. Proxies are useful because they make complex phenomena measurable, but they can also distort the picture. Attendance does not reveal whether students are intellectually involved, and hospital admissions may reflect access to care as well as disease prevalence. A proxy becomes especially misleading when institutions begin optimizing the measure itself. If a school is rewarded only for attendance, it may overlook the quality of learning. Responsible measurement therefore requires asking not only whether a metric is reliable, but also what aspect of reality it leaves out and how people might respond to the incentives it creates.

content: According to Reading Text C, why can a wetland fail to recover its former biodiversity even when its water level returns?
options: Water level has no relationship with wetlands.
Other factors, including invasive species and fragmented surrounding habitats, also influence recovery.
Native plants always prevent recovery.
Engineering interventions eliminate all ecological interactions.
passage: Restoring a wetland is sometimes presented as a straightforward engineering task: remove barriers, reintroduce native plants, and allow water to return. In practice, ecological recovery is less predictable. Hydrology, soil conditions, species interactions, and nearby land use can all shape the outcome. A site may regain its original water level yet fail to recover its former biodiversity if invasive species dominate or if surrounding habitats remain fragmented. For this reason, restoration projects increasingly use adaptive management. Managers define measurable objectives, monitor indicators over time, and revise interventions when evidence suggests that an approach is not working. Adaptive management does not eliminate uncertainty; it makes uncertainty part of the decision process. Its success depends on transparent monitoring and a willingness to change course rather than defend an initial plan.
